items.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024
items.q: It was a ballet version of “Carmen.” ... in this particular version of “Carmen” Carmen does not get killed...

ctx.x: I wonder if there’s a part of the music, if we separate the sections of music like the melody and the rhythm and the harmony, is there something when you’re writing for dance that you do less of? For instance because there’s an audio and a visual, do you need to spend as much time and effort on the melodic quality of the music if people are dancing to it?

Interestingly enough I did many projects where I was given video to score to. The most beautiful collaboration I had, I just had with this Cuban choreographer from London who did the San Francisco Ballet commission. And what was beautiful about it was we sat down for a week in my studio in UCLA and talked about the narrative and specifically designed characteristics for each of the players in the narrative so that all of a sudden I found myself literally planning and writing the music as the choreography was…

human being who is — you know who is so chained down. So even as I’m writing this ballet, with a fantastic ballet company and a fantastic symphony orchestra and a fantastic operatic setting, I found it incredibly freeing because I knew that with all these contractions, with all these straight jackets, that I was only going to be able to be myself. That was the only way I was going to be able to do it authentically. And so I did some of my most — I think I did some of my most honest composition in the midst of…
